DOCUMENT:
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [misread_evidence] at: "Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place." -- Table 1 shows mushroom risotto has the highest gross margin on the menu (80%); the weakest is sirloin steak (60%). Lowest sales is correct (90 plates, tied with specials), but the margin claim misreads the table.
2. [missing_consideration] at: "The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target." -- The projection uses current food costs, but section 4 states beef prices rise 12% from 1 April, the same date as the new prices. Burgers and steaks (380 plates a week) would see higher food costs (e.g. about £1.25 more per steak), eroding much of the projected gain; the margin and profit projections never account for it.
3. [inconsistency] at: "keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week" -- Section 2 says the restaurant is open Wednesday to Sunday, i.e. five days a week; the recommendation refers to six trading days.

REVIEW:
# Review: Menu Pricing Review, Spring 2026

The till data and competitor check are a reasonable basis for a pricing review. However, several conclusions do not follow from the paper's own figures. The most serious problems are that the risotto proposal contradicts Table 1, and the profit and margin projections leave out the beef cost rise the paper itself reports.

## Major issues

**1. The risotto has the highest margin on the menu, not the weakest (§5.2).**
Table 1 gives the risotto an 80% margin, the highest of any dish. Its cash profit per plate is £14.00 − £2.80 = £11.20, which is mid-table:

| Dish | Profit per plate |
|---|---|
| Steak | £15.60 |
| Fish and chips | £11.40 |
| Risotto | £11.20 |
| Curry | £10.90 |
| Burger | £10.80 |

Its 90 plates a week ties with specials, so it is not uniquely the lowest seller either. The proposed replacement is a seasonal special, and specials run at 64%. Swapping one for the other would therefore lower the margin.

There is also an unexamined risk. The risotto appears to be the only vegetarian main on the fixed menu. Removing it could cost whole tables where one diner is vegetarian, not just 90 plates. This proposal needs to be withdrawn or re-argued from scratch.

**2. The beef cost increase is left out of the projection (§4 vs §5.3).**
§4 reports that beef rises 12% from 1 April, the same day the new prices take effect. §5.3 still assumes the full price rise is extra profit. The added cost is:

- Burger: £4.20 × 12% ≈ £0.50 per plate × 260 ≈ £131 a week
- Steak: £10.40 × 12% ≈ £1.25 per plate × 120 ≈ £150 a week

That is about £281 a week, which cuts the £810 to roughly **£530 a week (about £27,500 a year)**.

**3. VAT is probably not accounted for.**
Menu prices are VAT-inclusive. If so, each £1 increase yields about £0.83 of net revenue. On that basis the gain becomes about £675 a week before the beef costs, and **about £395 a week (roughly £20,500 a year)** after them. That is under half the headline £42,000. The paper should state whether its figures are gross or net of VAT.

**4. The 71% margin claim does not hold.**
Using Table 1 and excluding specials (no price is given for them), the current main-course margin is about 69.9%. Applying the new prices but not the beef rise gives about 71.3%, which matches the paper. Including the beef rise brings it to about **69.7%, essentially unchanged**. Replacing the 80% risotto with a 64% special would pull it lower still. So the claim that these changes "help restore our 70% overall target" is not supported.

**5. Trading days are inconsistent.**
§2 says the restaurant is open Wednesday to Sunday, which is five days. §8 says "six trading days a week". This should be corrected, and the paper should confirm that "per week" figures and the ×52 annualisation use the correct basis.

## Weaker reasoning and claims

**6. "We remain the value option" overstates the position.**
The paper only claims prices stay below the competitor midpoint, and that is true:

| Dish | New price | Competitor midpoint |
|---|---|---|
| Fish and chips | £17.50 | ≈ £17.98 |
| Burger | £16.00 | £16.50 |
| Steak | £28.00 | £29.50 |

But all three new prices exceed the cheapest competitor (£16.95, £15.50 and £27.00). The restaurant would move from cheapest in the group to mid-pack. That is a real change in positioning and should be stated plainly.

**7. "Volumes will hold" is asserted, not evidenced.**
- A 60% repeat-guest base cuts both ways. Regulars are the people most likely to notice price increases.
- The evidence that the 2024 price change had "no visible effect" is anecdotal. No figures are given.
- No volume sensitivity is shown. A simple break-even would help: after beef costs, how many plates could be lost before the increase stops paying for itself?

**8. The baseline period is seasonal and short.**
January and February are typically quiet months. Comparing April and May against that baseline will likely show higher volumes for seasonal reasons alone, which could hide real volume losses. A same-period comparison with spring 2025 would be more reliable.

**9. Monitoring has no decision rule.**
§6 commits to eight weeks of tracking but does not say what drop in volume would trigger action, or what that action would be. Without this, the monitoring is not really an early warning system.

**10. Minor points:**
- **Fish costs:** Fish is the biggest seller, and §4 calls fish prices "volatile". The risk from a fish cost spike is not discussed.
- **Specials data:** The author's description says the data covers "every main course", but specials have no price or cost given.
- **Scope of the target:** The 70% target applies to all courses, but the review only covers mains.

## Summary

The burger, steak and fish price increases may still be justified, particularly to offset the beef rise. However, the case for them should be restated with corrected numbers:

- Net of VAT and beef costs, the gain is likely about £20,000–£28,000 a year, not £42,000.
- The main-course margin stays roughly flat, rather than rising to 71%.

The risotto removal is based on a misreading of Table 1 and should not be approved as written. Before resubmitting, the author should also:

- fix the trading-days figure
- add a volume break-even
- use a seasonally matched baseline
- set clear thresholds for action during monitoring
